title: The Jewish calendar
hook: a lunar year with a leap month seven times in nineteen years, so festivals keep their seasons

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bedtime Shema: the last words of the day, and a quiet line forgiving anyone who hurt you. Your line was forgive before sleeping. Did you let one thing go last night? Day one hundred twenty-one.

Ask a Jewish friend when Hanukkah is this year, and there's a good chance they'll have to look it up. One year it starts in late November. Another year it lands right on top of Christmas. Passover drifts around March and April. Rosh Hashanah can come in early September or in October. It looks like the holidays wander. They don't. They're keeping time, just not by the clock on your phone. For the next few weeks we walk through the Jewish year, one holiday at a time, as they arrive. And before any holiday, you need the thing that holds them all.
screen: `WHEN IS HANUKKAH THIS YEAR?` → `THE HOLIDAYS SEEM TO WANDER.` → `THEY'RE KEEPING A DIFFERENT CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word for a calendar is luach. It means a tablet or a board, the same word used for the tablets Moses carried down the mountain. Today a luach is often a printed calendar on a synagogue wall, or an app. The Jewish calendar runs on the moon. Each month begins at the new moon and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days, because that's how long the moon takes to go from dark to dark. In the first chapter of Genesis, the lights in the sky are made "for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years." And the Psalms say it plainly: "Who appointedst the moon for seasons." Here's the problem. Twelve moon months fall about eleven days short of the sun's year. A purely lunar calendar slides backward through the seasons, and the Torah ties Passover to spring and Sukkot to the harvest. So the Jewish calendar does something clever: seven times in every nineteen years, it adds a whole extra month, a second Adar, in late winter. That leap month pulls the moon back in line with the sun, and Passover stays in spring. For centuries, a new month was declared by a court in Jerusalem when witnesses reported seeing the thin new moon. Later, tradition says in the fourth century, the calendar was fixed by calculation, so Jews scattered around the world could keep the same days. Two more things. A Jewish day begins at sunset, because Genesis says "there was evening and there was morning." And the years are counted from creation, as the rabbis reckoned it, which is why a Hebrew year number runs into the five thousands.
screen: `LUACH: A TABLET, A CALENDAR.` · `EACH MONTH BEGINS AT THE NEW MOON.` · `A LEAP MONTH, SEVEN TIMES IN NINETEEN.` · `THE DAY BEGINS AT SUNSET.` · then, large: `THE MOON FOR SEASONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find today's Hebrew date. Afterward, look it up on any Jewish calendar or online. For now, settle, and breathe. Notice the time of day you're in. If it's evening, remember that on this calendar, tomorrow has already begun. Think of one date that matters to you, a birthday, an anniversary, the day someone died. Wonder what it was on the moon's calendar. Just hold the idea that there's more than one way to count a life. The bell holds the time.
Luach. A tablet, and the Jewish calendar: moon months, kept in step with the sun by a leap month seven times in nineteen years.
Your line: the moon keeps time. Tonight, notice where the day ends: watch the sun go down and say, quietly, a new day starts now. Day one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish communities keep a lunisolar calendar: months follow the moon, a second Adar is added seven times in nineteen years, and each day, Shabbat and festival begins at sunset. Many families keep a printed luach from their synagogue.

fork.setup: you're keeping a calendar of moon months, and Passover must stay in spring. after a few years it's drifting toward winter. what do you do?
options: drop the moon and count by the sun alone.
add a whole extra month every few years.
let Passover drift through the seasons.
fork.reveal: the Jewish calendar adds a second Adar seven times in nineteen years, so the moon keeps the months and the festivals keep their seasons.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 1:14, 1:5 and Psalms 104:19.
Luach also means the tablets of the covenant (luchot, e.g. Exodus 34:1); confirm the framing 'the same word'.
Fixed calendar attributed by tradition to Hillel II, around 359 CE; stated as 'tradition says in the fourth century'.
Year 5787 began at Rosh Hashanah in September 2026; confirm, and note this line dates the script.
Leap years in the 19-year cycle: years 3, 6, 8, 11, 14, 17, 19 (Adar I added).
Review pass: hook said 'last year it was early December', which was wrong for 2025 (Hanukkah began December 14) and dated the script; changed to 'one year it starts in late November' (e.g. 2013).

Editor review (days 113–131): 'the year that began this September is 5787' removed, since it dates the script and is wrong in every later year; now 'a Hebrew year number runs into the five thousands'. The '354 days' figure cut (only the eleven-day gap is kept, which the leap-month explanation needs); 'keeping perfect time' softened, since the fixed calendar drifts slightly against the sun over centuries. The note above about 5787 no longer applies.
